To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

age interactions for breast cancer risk factors can be both qualitative (reversing) and quantitative (non-crossovers), and that the reversal (crossover) pattern of age interactions is more common among younger women.
age-specific breast cancer relative risks are not constant and that they may change direction with age.
age interactions are common for breast cancer risk factors and are often non-monotonic, with crossover points that vary according to the risk factor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of etiologic clues and the development of descriptive tools to characterize age interactions.
the development of a descriptive tool that can be used to identify age interactions and to clarify breast cancer risk factors and etiologies.
identifying age-specific risks and interactions that may help elucidate breast cancer etiology and improve prevention efforts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the age-specific relative risk of breast cancer is not constant and varies according to the specific risk factor.
the age interactions for all breast cancer risk factors were statistically significant and non-linear.
the etiologic role of risk factors is not uniform throughout the female breast cancer life course.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
breast cancer risk is not a simple function of age.
breast cancer risks are highest in women ages 40 years and older and are elevated by the presence of risk factors.
age-specific breast cancer rates are highly dependent upon the covariate of interest and age.
The main takeaway from our work is that
age-specific breast cancer risk estimates are needed to identify age interactions, which in turn may provide important etiological clues.
the age-specific nature of breast cancer risks should not be assumed, and that it is important to consider age-specific risks in breast cancer studies.
age-specific risks and interactions are important for etiologic studies and for the identification of high risk subgroups for prevention and screening.
